BPM Justification: Adding a compensating activity that runs alongside an otherwise-frozen process is a legitimate, if narrow, process-modeling pattern (an auxiliary activity with its own trigger), but its purpose here is purely offsetting environmental impact rather than changing process behavior, so structurally it's a minor addition rather than a core design concern.

Restructuring a choreography or swapping which partner performs which part of a collaboration is squarely a process-collaboration/choreography-modeling concern, one of the more advanced but well-established areas of BPM, independent of why the swap is being made.

Offering two functionally-equivalent process paths and letting the owner or customer pick between them is a straightforward variant/branching decision at the process model level (a decision gateway plus a second flow), which is bread-and-butter process design regardless of what distinguishes the two variants.

Deciding whether an activity is a service task or a user task, i.e. automated vs. human-performed, is one of the most basic and frequent modeling decisions in any BPMN diagram; the environmental motivation behind the choice doesn't change that this is core process design.

This is just the automation-vs-human decision made in the other direction, and reversing a task's performer type is exactly as much a modeling concern as the forward case; nothing about the sustainability rationale changes its structural weight in the process.

Standard process optimization techniques (removing redundant steps, reducing cycle time) are core BPM analysis/optimization work, and I'll grant this is relevant because it's literally that work; but tacking on an environmental KPI alongside the usual ones doesn't in itself introduce any new modeling or execution concept, so I don't rate it as high as the guidelines that change control flow or task assignment.

Centralizing previously outsourced work back in-house does restructure a choreography and can shift task ownership across organizational boundaries, which is a real process-design concern, but as stated the guideline is mostly a sourcing/governance decision with only a secondary, indirect effect on the process model itself.

Swapping which electricity, materials, or hosting an activity's underlying resource uses is a resource-configuration change beneath the task, not a change to the process model, control flow, or task assignment at all; from a process-design standpoint this is generic infrastructure/procurement substitution that happens to be attached to a task.

Choosing which visible green features to add to a product for marketing/reputation purposes is a product-design and communications decision that doesn't touch process structure, task assignment, or execution at all; there's no process-modeling artifact here for a BPM practitioner to act on.
